entry.englishMeaning: to force one’s progress by intimidating or dominating others
entry.coreIdea: Get your way by pressuring people instead of winning their agreement.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Figurative description of making progress by intimidation: force a way through opposition rather than gain cooperation.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Negative: “bully” presents the method as domineering or unfair.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Self-critical here: “we try” includes the writer among people who resort to intimidation.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Natural in everyday criticism and discussion of behaviour. In diplomatic feedback, describe the pressure used rather than label a person a bully.

when_to_use: Use this expression critically when someone gets through a discussion or process by intimidating others.
It can describe using status, threats or aggressive demands to overcome objections.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it simply for working hard through a difficult task; it implies pressure on other people.
A firm but respectful argument is not necessarily bullying. Describe the actual behaviour before making this accusation.

advanced_nuance: Bully one's way through strongly criticizes the method used to get a result. It does not simply mean being confident or persistent.
The expression can describe an unsuccessful attempt: trying to bully your way through does not mean that others eventually agree.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture someone forcing a decision by shouting down objections.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: He tried to bully his way through the discussion, but the chair stopped him.
memory_practice.recall_question: Does bullying your way through a discussion suggest respectful persuasion or intimidation?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which fits the expression? A: Listening carefully and answering objections. B: Threatening colleagues until they give in. Explain what makes the behaviour bullying.
memory_practice.production_task: Describe a fictional meeting to a colleague. Use a natural form of bully one's way through and name the intimidating behaviour you observed.

examples.example_1: He tried to bully his way through the meeting by threatening anyone who disagreed.
examples.example_2: You cannot bully your way through negotiations and expect the other side to trust you.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: He says he'll cancel our funding unless we agree immediately.
B: He is trying to bully his way through the discussion.
A: Let's ask for the proposal in writing before we respond.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: We  try  to  bully  our  way  through .
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to force one’s progress by intimidating or dominating others
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speakers describe trying to make progress by intimidating or dominating other people. The short sentence does not say who is being pressured.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: “She bullied his way through the meeting” when she is the person forcing her own progress.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say: “She bullied her way through the meeting.” The possessive in bully one's way through normally refers to the subject.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Persuading people aims to gain agreement through reasons; bullying one's way through relies on intimidation or domination.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: bully one's way through + discussion/process; change one's to my, your, his, her, our or their
common_collocations: bully your way through a meeting

entry.englishMeaning: the ability or practice of controlling behaviour and working consistently toward a goal
entry.coreIdea: Keep doing what your goal requires, even when you would rather stop.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract quality of self-control and consistent effort; here, a quality praised in colleagues' work.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Positive in this sense: discipline supports dependable effort rather than referring to punishment.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Appreciative here: the authors explicitly thank their colleagues for this quality.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral and natural in education, work and personal development. Specify “self-discipline” when confusion with punishment is possible.

when_to_use: Use discipline for self-control that helps someone keep working toward a goal.
It fits routines such as regular study, saving money or finishing demanding work.
when_not_to_use: Do not assume discipline means punishment in this sentence; the writers are praising a personal quality.
A sudden burst of enthusiasm does not by itself show the steady self-control meant here.

advanced_nuance: Discipline emphasizes consistent self-control; it does not imply that the person lacks creativity. The source praises both qualities together.
In this sense discipline is normally uncountable. A discipline meaning a field of study is a separate sense.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture a small daily practice session marked on a calendar.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: Discipline keeps me practising even when I do not feel motivated.
memory_practice.recall_question: How can discipline help on a day when motivation is low?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which shows discipline? A: Studying only when excited about a subject. B: Keeping a realistic study routine even on less exciting days. Explain your choice.
memory_practice.production_task: Tell a friend how a fictional learner maintains a study habit. Use discipline and describe one regular action.

examples.example_1: It takes discipline to study every evening after a long day at work.
examples.example_2: She showed discipline by following her savings plan instead of buying things she did not need.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: How did you finish the course while working full-time?
B: Discipline helped. I studied for half an hour before breakfast each day.
A: I'll try setting a regular time too.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: First,  to  our  colleagues  at  Vi talSmarts,  we  ex press  apprecia­ tion  for  creativ ity,  discipline,  competence,  and  friend ship.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: the ability or practice of controlling behaviour and working consistently toward a goal
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The writers thank their colleagues for controlled, consistent effort alongside creativity and competence.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: “She has many discipline” for this quality. Discipline is uncountable in the self-control sense.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say: “She has a lot of discipline” or “She shows great discipline.”
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Motivation is the desire or reason to act. Discipline helps you keep acting even when that desire is weak.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: have/show discipline; have the discipline to + verb; it takes discipline to + verb

entry.englishMeaning: a problem or condition that makes an agreement or choice unacceptable
entry.coreIdea: Picture one condition stopping a handshake.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract compound: a condition serious enough to make someone reject an agreement or option.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Strongly negative toward the condition: it signals that the problem crosses an acceptance limit.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Firm but conditional here: “would be” identifies a clause the speaker could not accept.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in workplace negotiation and everyday choices. “An unacceptable condition” is a more formal alternative.

when_to_use: Explain politely why an unpredictable cancellation fee is a deal-breaker.
A natural model: The lack of evening transport is a deal-breaker for me.
when_not_to_use: A drawback reduces attractiveness; a deal-breaker rules the option out.
Use it only for a decisive barrier, or it can make a negotiable concern sound final.

advanced_nuance: deal-breaker: Use it only for a decisive barrier, or it can make a negotiable concern sound final.

entry.coreIdea: Yes to the fact, still a different conclusion.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Logical connector expressing concession: the unavoidable delay does not remove the duty to inform the customer.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: it marks a contrast between a difficulty and what should still have happened.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Measured and corrective here: the speaker accepts the delay but criticizes the lack of communication.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral and natural in speech or writing. “Nevertheless” usually sounds more formal.

when_to_use: Accept that a delay was unavoidable while explaining why notice was needed. A model in this sense: The tickets were expensive. Even so, the concert was worth it.
when_not_to_use: Even so refers back to a stated situation; even if introduces a possible condition.
It concedes the previous point without allowing it to settle the conclusion.

advanced_nuance: even so: It concedes the previous point without allowing it to settle the conclusion.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Yes to the fact, still a different conclusion.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: The tickets were expensive. Even so, the concert was worth it.
memory_practice.production_task: Accept that a delay was unavoidable while explaining why notice was needed. Respond in one or two natural sentences using the expression, then compare with the pattern after answering.
memory_practice.recall_question: Recall the expression for this meaning without looking: despite the situation just described. Explain its function in one sentence.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which option fits the taught meaning and standard construction? A: The expense was high. Even so, it was worth it. B: Even so the expense, it was worth it. Explain your choice, then check the correction and distinction.

examples.another_setting: The tickets were expensive. Even so, the concert was worth it.

B: I agree, though we should budget earlier next time.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Even so the expense, it was worth it.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Even so refers back to a stated situation; even if introduces a possible condition.

entry.englishMeaning: to present an idea or proposal in an attempt to persuade others
entry.coreIdea: Present an idea in a way intended to win support.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract verb for presenting a proposal persuasively; here, the CEO puts forward his preferred option.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral as an act of persuasion; the narrator's “unpopular” and “potentially disastrous” supply the criticism.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Critical toward the proposal here, because the narrator describes its reception and possible consequences negatively.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in business and creative work, and conversational elsewhere. “Present” is a less promotional alternative.

when_to_use: Use pitch when presenting a proposal with the aim of gaining support, approval or funding.
You can pitch a business idea, an article or a plan to a person or group.
when_not_to_use: If you are simply reporting facts without trying to win support, explain or report may be more accurate.
In very formal correspondence, propose or present may sound less conversational.

advanced_nuance: Pitch describes an attempt to persuade, not a successful sale or approval. An audience can reject an idea after hearing it pitched.
The source's criticism concerns Chris's proposal. Pitch itself does not say whether an idea is good, bad or popular.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Picture explaining your proposal and why someone should support it.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: I pitched a cheaper transport plan to the team.
memory_practice.recall_question: What response do you usually hope for when you pitch an idea?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which is a pitch? A: Listing yesterday's events without a request. B: Explaining a new plan and asking a manager to back it. Explain the difference.
memory_practice.production_task: Tell a colleague about a fictional proposal you intend to present. Use pitch, name your audience and say what support you want.

examples.example_1: She pitched a weekend reading club to the library manager.
examples.example_2: The team will pitch its new delivery service to potential investors tomorrow.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Can we get support for the reading club?
B: I'll pitch the idea to the library manager on Friday.
A: Take the list of interested families with you.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: MAST ERING  CRUCIAL  CONVE RSATI ONS  19  Then  Chri s,  the  CEO,  pitched  his  prefer ence-one  that  was  both  unpopular  and  potentially  disastrous.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to present an idea or proposal in an attempt to persuade others
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: Chris presented his preferred option to persuade others to support it. The writer describes that option as unpopular and potentially disastrous.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Less natural with a short object: “She pitched to the manager her idea.” The usual order places the idea before the audience.
mistakes_differences.correction: Use the usual order: “She pitched her idea to the manager.” Pitch comes before the idea, followed by to and the audience.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Pitch adds a persuasive purpose to presenting an idea. Mention only says that you referred to it, without necessarily asking for support.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: pitch + idea/proposal + to + audience; pitch an idea to someone
